steps.user_message: I need help with my 2023 tax return. I'm head of household in Boston MA. My W-2 from Riverside Hospital shows $64,800. I had $12,500 in 1099 income (IT contracting, 2 clients), $1,560 from Goldman Sachs Marcus, and $290 from TD Ameritrade. I have a home office (140 sq ft, exclusive use); rent is $1,720/month for 620 sq ft total. Student loan interest: $3,600 (FedLoan, 2016–2020). I donated $1,350 to St. Mary's Food Bank (have the receipt) have receipt, and had $1,350 in work expenses. What can I deduct, and should I itemize or take the standard deduction? What forms do I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Here’s a clear breakdown for your 2023 return (federal first, then Massachusetts), plus the forms you’ll need.

Short answer:
- Federal: You should take the standard deduction (Head of Household: $20,800). Itemizing won’t beat it with the info provided.
- You can deduct your Schedule C business expenses (including a sizable home office deduction using the actual-expense method), half of your self-employment tax, up to $2,500 of student loan interest (you appear to qualify for the full amount), and you’ll likely get a QBI deduction on your business income.
- Massachusetts: You can likely claim the MA renter deduction (up to $3,000) and MA charitable contributions even if you take the federal standard deduction.

What you can deduct (federal)
- Standard vs. itemized
  - Standard deduction (Head of Household, 2023): $20,800.
  - Your potential itemized deductions listed: $1,350 charitable. No mortgage interest or property tax provided; rent doesn’t count federally. So itemizing would be far below $20,800 → take the standard deduction.
- Self-employment (1099) deductions on Schedule C
  - Home office (actual method is best for you):
    - Size: 140 sq ft exclusive use
    - Home size: 620 sq ft → business use % ≈ 22.6%
    - Rent: $1,720/month → $20,640/year
    - Deductible rent portion ≈ 22.6% × $20,640 ≈ $4,660 as an indirect expense.
    - You can also include a business share of utilities, renter’s insurance, internet/phone, etc., if applicable (not provided). These would further increase the deduction.
    - Note: The home office deduction can’t create a Schedule C loss; any excess carries forward.
  - Other business expenses: If your $1,350 “work expenses” were for your IT contracting (not your W‑2 job), you can deduct them on Schedule C. If they were for your W‑2 job, they aren’t deductible federally for 2023.
- Self-employment tax and related deduction
  - You’ll owe SE tax on your net Schedule C profit. Half of your SE tax is an “above-the-line” deduction.
  - Ballpark with the info given:
    - If $1,350 “work expenses” are business-related: net profit ≈ $12,500 − $4,660 − $1,350 = $6,490; SE tax ≈ $917; half deductible ≈ $458.
    - If they’re not business-related: net profit ≈ $12,500 − $4,660 = $7,840; SE tax ≈ $1,107; half deductible ≈ $553.
- Student loan interest (Form 1098-E)
  - You paid $3,600; the federal deduction caps at $2,500 and phases out for HOH MAGI between $75,000–$90,000.
  - With your deductions (especially the home office), your MAGI likely stays under $75,000, so you can probably take the full $2,500.
- Charitable contributions ($1,350 to St. Mary’s Food Bank)
  - Deductible only if you itemize federally. Since you’ll take the standard deduction, you won’t claim this on your federal Schedule A.
- Interest/dividends
  - $1,560 from Goldman Sachs Marcus (taxable interest) and $290 from TD Ameritrade (likely interest or ordinary dividends). These are taxable; because your interest exceeds $1,500, you’ll file Schedule B.
- QBI deduction (Section 199A)
  - You likely qualify for the 20% QBI deduction on your qualified business income since you’re under the 2023 HOH threshold.
  - Ballpark: If net profit ≈ $6,490 and half SE tax ≈ $458, QBI ≈ $6,032 → QBI deduction ≈ $1,206. If net profit ≈ $7,840, QBI deduction ~ $1,450. Exact amount depends on your final numbers.

Massachusetts (high level)
- File MA Form 1 (resident).
- Renter deduction: You can deduct 50% of MA rent paid, up to $3,000. With $20,640 rent, you’ll hit the $3,000 cap.
- Charitable contributions: MA allows a charitable deduction for 2023 even if you don’t itemize federally—save that $1,350 receipt.
- MA doesn’t allow the federal QBI deduction.
- Interest/dividends and business income are generally taxable in MA; rates and treatment differ from federal on certain items.

Forms you’ll need (federal)
- Form 1040 (Head of Household filing status)
- Schedule 1 (Adjustments, including student loan interest and half SE tax; also where 1099-NEC income flows via Schedule C)
- Schedule B (you have >$1,500 of interest)
- Schedule C (sole proprietorship for your IT contracting; both clients can go on one Schedule C if it’s the same business)
- Schedule SE (self-employment tax)
- Form 8829 (home office actual expenses). If you used the simplified method, you’d just enter it on Schedule C line 30, but the actual method is better for you.
- Form 8995 (QBI deduction)
- Schedule A only if itemizing (you likely won’t)

Common MA forms
- Form 1 (resident return)
- Schedule Y (other deductions), where renter and charitable deductions are typically claimed

Quick next steps
- Confirm whether the $1,350 “work expenses” were for your 1099 contracting or your W‑2 job.
- Gather any additional business expenses (utilities, renter’s insurance, internet/phone business share, supplies, mileage, software, etc.) to maximize Schedule C and potentially strengthen student loan interest eligibility.
- Keep your 1098-E (student loan interest), 1099-INT/1099-DIV/1099-NEC, and your charitable receipt.

If you confirm the nature of the $1,350 “work expenses,” I can refine the estimates and walk you line-by-line through the key forms.
